tool.name: Ruby
tool.tagline: Expressive, object-oriented language designed for programmer happiness
tool.description: Ruby is a dynamic, fully object-oriented language with a clean syntax built around blocks and message passing. It powers Ruby on Rails and tools like Homebrew, Jekyll and Chef, and is loved for scripting and DSLs. Learning Ruby teaches you a flexible object model and an idiomatic, collection-oriented style that carries over to many languages.

glossary.def: Interactive Ruby: a prompt you start by typing irb in a terminal. Each line of Ruby you type runs at once and shows its result.
A way to write several lines of text in Ruby code: start with <<~NAME, write the lines, and end with NAME on a line of its own.
A fixed name in Ruby written with a leading colon, like :status. The same symbol is always the very same object, so symbols are used as labels and hash keys.
The * in front of a Ruby parameter or value: it gathers several values into one array, or spreads an array out into separate values. A double splat, **, does the same for keyword arguments.
In Ruby, a chunk of code written in { } or between do and end and handed to a method, which can run it once, many times or not at all.
A Ruby variable whose name starts with @. It belongs to one object and holds that object's own data.
The object a method is called on: in "hi".upcase, the receiver is "hi".
Ruby's built-in module of collection methods (map, select, sort, sum and dozens more). Any class that defines each can include it and get them all.
Ruby's built-in module that gives a class <, >, between? and clamp, once the class defines how to compare two objects with <=>.
A Ruby object that represents a walk through a sequence of values and hands them out one at a time on request; it can even describe an endless sequence.
A Ruby object holding a block of code, so it can be stored in a variable and run later with call. A lambda is a stricter kind of proc.
How many arguments a method, block or lambda expects.
The Ruby error class that ordinary program errors inherit from. A rescue with no class name catches it and everything that inherits from it.
A packaged Ruby library with a name and a version, installed from rubygems.org with the gem or bundle command.
Ruby's package system: the public site rubygems.org where gems are published, and the gem command that installs them.
The standard Ruby tool that installs the gems a project lists in its Gemfile, records their exact versions, and makes the program use those versions.
A file at the root of a Ruby project that lists the gems the project needs and which versions are acceptable.
The file Bundler writes listing the exact version of every gem it installed, so every computer runs the project with the same ones.
A small script in a project's bin folder, like bin/rails, that runs a tool with the project's locked gem versions.
The most popular web framework written in Ruby, used to build web applications backed by a database.
The testing library that ships with Ruby: tests are classes whose test_ methods check results with assert methods.
A popular Ruby testing library whose tests read like sentences: describe a thing, say what it should do, and expect a result.
The ordered list of classes and modules Ruby searches when a method is called: the object's class, the modules it includes, its parent class, and so on up to BasicObject.
A hidden class Ruby gives a single object, holding methods that belong to that object alone. A class's own methods (class methods) live in its singleton class.
A method defined on one particular object rather than on its class, like def obj.shout.
Reopening an existing class, often one built into the language like String, and adding or changing its methods for the whole program.
A Ruby way to add or change methods of a class only in files that switch it on with using, instead of for the whole program like monkey patching.
The main Ruby implementation, written in C, that you get from ruby-lang.org. Most Ruby code runs on it. Also called MRI.
Part of a gem written in the C language instead of Ruby, built for speed or to use an existing C library.
Global VM Lock: CRuby's rule that only one thread runs Ruby code at a time in a process. A thread waiting for files or the network lets go of it. Python's version is called the GIL.
An experimental Ruby unit of work that can run at the same time as others on different CPU cores. Ractors share no changeable objects; they pass messages instead.
A lightweight Ruby task that runs until it pauses itself and carries on when resumed. Many fibers can take turns on one thread.
A Ruby hook that, when a fiber would sit waiting for a file or the network, pauses it and runs other fibers until the data is ready.
CRuby's built-in just-in-time compiler: while the program runs, it turns frequently used Ruby methods into machine code so they run faster.
CRuby's record of which instance variables an object has, in what order, which lets it find them quickly.
In Ruby, a name that starts with a capital letter, like MAX_SIZE, for a value meant to stay fixed. Ruby warns you if you assign it again.
In Ruby pattern matching, a description of a value's shape, like { name: String }, that is checked against a value and can name its parts.
One of the alternative paths in an if, case or case/in; only one of them runs.
To unpack a collection into separate variables in one step, as in first, *rest = list.
A way of collecting garbage: first mark every object the program can still reach, then sweep away (free) everything left unmarked.
A small check CRuby runs whenever an old object is changed to point at a newer one, so the garbage collector doesn't miss that link.
In Ruby's garbage collector, new objects form the young generation, checked often; objects that survive several collections join the old generation, checked less often.
The first runs of a program or benchmark, while YJIT is still compiling the busy code; they are slower than later runs.
Something only one thread can hold at a time; the others wait until it is released. Used to stop threads from changing the same data at once.

concepts.name: Running Ruby
concepts.summary: Run your first Ruby program, try lines out in IRB, print values with puts and p, and call methods on objects.
concepts.why: Every Ruby journey starts with running code and looking at what it produces, and IRB is where Rubyists try ideas out.
concepts.body:
A program is a list of instructions for a computer, written in a **programming language**: a precise language the computer can follow. Ruby is one, designed to read almost like English. You write Ruby in an ordinary text file whose name ends in `.rb`, such as `hello.rb`. A short program kept in one file like this is often called a **script**.

To run it, open a **terminal**: a window where you type commands instead of clicking (Terminal on macOS, PowerShell on Windows). Typing `ruby hello.rb` and pressing Enter makes Ruby carry out the file's lines from top to bottom. `ruby -v` shows which version of Ruby you have.

For quick experiments there is **IRB** (Interactive Ruby). Type `irb` in the terminal, then type one line of Ruby and press Enter: the result appears straight away, like a calculator that speaks Ruby. Try `2 + 3`. Type `exit` to leave.

Text in a program goes between quotes, like `"Hello"`. Programmers call a piece of text a **string** (a string of characters). Numbers are written plainly: `42`, `3.5`.

Three commands show things on the screen:

- `puts x` prints `x`, then starts a new line.
- `print x` prints it and stays on the same line.
- `p x` prints an exact view meant for programmers: text keeps its quotes, so you can tell the text `"42"` from the number `42`.

That makes `p` the favourite tool for **debugging**: hunting down a mistake in a program (a **bug**) by looking at what values really are.

In Ruby every value, whether a number or a piece of text, is an **object**: a thing that knows how to do certain jobs. You ask an object to do a job by writing a dot and the job's name: `"ruby".upcase` gives `"RUBY"`, and `5.even?` answers `false`. Each such job is called a **method**. Even `1 + 2` is really the method `+` called on `1`.

A line starting with `#` is a comment: a note for humans that Ruby skips. Parentheses around what you give a method are optional: `puts "hi"` and `puts("hi")` do the same.

A `?` at the end of a method name marks a question that answers `true` or `false`, like `empty?`. A `!` marks a version that changes the object itself instead of giving you a changed copy, like `upcase!`.
concepts.code:
# hello.rb: run it by typing `ruby hello.rb` in the terminal
puts "Hello, Ruby!"        # Hello, Ruby!
puts RUBY_VERSION          # the Ruby version, e.g. 3.4.7

puts "42"                  # 42
p "42"                     # "42"  (p keeps the quotes: this is text)
p 42                       # 42    (this is a number)

puts 5.even?               # false
puts "ruby".upcase         # RUBY
puts "ruby".length         # 4
puts 1.+(2)                # 3: even + is a method
puts 42.class              # Integer (what kind of object 42 is)
takeaways: Run a file with ruby file.rb; try single lines in irb
puts shows a value plainly; p shows exactly what it is, quotes included
Every value is an object, and you call its methods with a dot
pitfalls: Checking a value with puts and missing that it is text rather than a number, or empty; p shows exactly what is there.

quiz.q: What does p "hi" print?
quiz.explain: p prints the exact programmer's view, which keeps the quotes around text.

quiz.q: In "ruby".upcase, what is upcase?
options: A method: a job the string object knows how to do
quiz.explain: The dot asks the object on its left to run the method named on its right.

concepts.name: Variables, numbers and nil
concepts.summary: Store values in variables and meet Ruby's basic kinds of value: whole numbers, decimals, text, true/false and nil.
concepts.why: Every calculation and every yes-or-no decision in a program depends on these values and on Ruby's simple rule for what counts as true.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name for a value, like a labelled jar: `count = 3` puts 3 in a jar called `count`, and later `count + 1` gives 4. The `=` means "store this", not "is equal to". You can put a new value in the same jar at any time: `count = 10`.

Names are lowercase words joined by underscores, like `total_price`. A name starting with a capital letter, like `MAX_SIZE = 10`, is a **constant**: meant to stay fixed, so Ruby warns if you change it.

Every value has a kind that decides what you can do with it. Numbers come in two kinds:

- An **integer** is a whole number: `7`, `-3`, or even `2**100` (`**` means "to the power of"; Ruby handles whole numbers of any size).
- A float is a number with a decimal point, like `9.5`. The name is short for **floating-point number**.

Two surprises. Dividing one integer by another gives an integer, throwing the leftover away: `7 / 2` is `3`. This is **integer division**; write `7.0 / 2` to get `3.5`. With negative numbers it rounds down, so `-7 / 2` is `-4`. And floats are stored approximately, so `0.1 + 0.2` shows `0.30000000000000004`, in every language; that is why money is often counted in whole cents.

Text values are strings, like `"Ada"`. Then come three special values. `true` and `false` are the answers to yes-or-no questions, called **booleans**. And `nil` means "no value at all", like an empty jar. Other languages call it **null**.

When Ruby checks a condition (written with `if`, next lesson), it needs a yes or a no. The rule is short: **only `false` and `nil` count as no**. Every other value, including `0` and empty text `""`, counts as yes. Values that count as yes are called **truthy**, the others falsy. Many languages treat `0` as no, so watch out. To ask "is this nil?" write `x.nil?`; to ask "is this text empty?" write `x.empty?`.

Values never change kind on their own; you convert them. `"42".to_i` turns text into the integer `42`, `"3.5".to_f` gives `3.5`, and `42.to_s` gives the text `"42"`. `to_i` is forgiving: `"12abc".to_i` quietly gives `12`. To check what a person typed, use the strict `Integer("12abc")`, which stops with an error (`ArgumentError`) instead of guessing.

A handy shortcut: `name ||= "guest"` stores `"guest"` only if `name` is currently `nil` or `false`, filling in a missing value. (The example also shows `&.`, which skips a method call on `nil`.)
concepts.code:
count = 3
count = count + 1
puts count               # 4
price = 9.5              # a float
puts 2**100              # 1267650600228229401496703205376
puts 7 / 2               # 3   (integer division drops the .5)
puts(-7 / 2)             # -4  (rounds down)
puts 7.fdiv(2)           # 3.5
puts 0.1 + 0.2           # 0.30000000000000004

puts "zero counts as yes" if 0   # zero counts as yes
p nil.nil?               # true
p "".empty?              # true

p "42".to_i + 1          # 43
p "12abc".to_i           # 12  (forgiving)
# Integer("12abc")       # would stop with ArgumentError (strict)

name = nil
name ||= "guest"
p name                   # "guest"
p nil&.length            # nil: &. skips the call on nil, no error
takeaways: Only false and nil count as no; 0 and "" count as yes
Integer division throws the leftover away: 7 / 2 is 3
Convert explicitly: to_i is forgiving, Integer() is strict
pitfalls: Writing if count to mean "if count is not zero": every number counts as yes, so write if count > 0 or if count.zero?.

quiz.q: Which of these values counts as no (falsy) in Ruby?
quiz.explain: Only nil and false count as no; every other value, including 0 and empty text, counts as yes.

quiz.q: What is -7 / 2 in Ruby?
quiz.explain: Dividing two integers gives a whole number, rounded down, so -3.5 becomes -4.

concepts.name: Conditionals, loops and case
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if, unless and case, and repeat work with while, until and times.
concepts.why: Choosing what to do and repeating work are the two basic steps behind almost every program, and Ruby's versions read almost like English.
concepts.body:
Programs make choices: if the score is high enough, say "pass", otherwise "fail". Code that only runs when a condition holds is a **conditional**:

```ruby
if score >= 50
  puts "pass"
elsif score >= 40
  puts "close"
else
  puts "fail"
end
```

`elsif` adds another check, `else` catches everything left over, and `end` closes the whole thing. `unless` is the opposite of `if`: `unless raining` means "if not raining".

Conditions are built with **operators**, signs that compare or combine values: `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. One `=` stores a value; two compare. Combine conditions with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not): `if age >= 18 && member`. Ruby also has the words `and`, `or` and `not`, but they behave subtly differently, so use the signs in conditions.

In Ruby an `if` is an **expression**: a piece of code that produces a value. So you can store its result: `label = if score > 50 then "pass" else "fail" end`. For tiny choices there is a shorthand: `score > 50 ? "pass" : "fail"`, read as "condition ? value if yes : value if no".

For a one-line action, put the condition after it: `puts "Bring a coat" if temp < 15`. This modifier form reads like English and is very common. Avoid `unless` with `else`; it is hard to follow.

`case` picks one of several options, like a menu:

```ruby
case day
when "Sat", "Sun" then "rest"
when "Fri" then "almost there"
else "work"
end
```

A `when` can also be a range of numbers (`when 1..12` means 1 to 12) or a kind of value (`when Integer`, meaning any whole number). Behind the scenes `case` compares with the operator `===`, which asks "does this fit?": is it inside the range, is it of that kind.

A **loop** repeats code. `while cond ... end` repeats as long as the condition is true, `until cond ... end` repeats until it becomes true, and `loop do ... end` repeats until you call `break`. Rubyists more often use counting helpers: `3.times { |i| puts i }` runs the code in braces three times, with `i` set to 0, 1 and 2.

One pass through a loop is called an **iteration**. Inside a loop, `next` skips to the next iteration and `break` stops the loop.
concepts.code:
temp = 12
if temp < 5
  puts "cold"
elsif temp < 20
  puts "mild"                # mild
else
  puts "warm"
end

puts "Bring a coat" if temp < 15   # Bring a coat
grade = 72 >= 70 ? "pass" : "fail"
puts grade                   # pass

age = 7
group = case age
        when 0..12 then "child"
        when 13..19 then "teen"
        else "adult"
        end
puts group                   # child

3.times { |i| print i, " " } # 0 1 2
puts
n = 0
n += 1 until n * n > 50      # n += 1 means n = n + 1
puts n                       # 8
takeaways: if/elsif/else/end and unless choose which code runs
if and case are expressions: they produce a value you can store
Prefer helpers like 3.times over hand-written while loops
pitfalls: Writing = (store) instead of == (compare) in a condition: if x = 5 stores 5 and always counts as yes.

quiz.q: Why does when Integer match 5 in a case?
options: case asks whether 5 is an Integer (a whole number), and it is
quiz.explain: case compares with ===, and for a kind of value like Integer that checks whether the value is one of that kind.

quiz.q: What does temp < 15 ? "coat" : "no coat" give when temp is 20?
quiz.explain: The condition is false, so the value after the colon is chosen.

concepts.name: Strings and symbols
concepts.summary: Build and change text with strings, know when a string can be changed in place, and use symbols as fixed names.
concepts.why: Almost every program reads, builds or prints text, and symbols appear in nearly every line of real Ruby code.
concepts.body:
A string is a piece of text in quotes. Double quotes let you insert values into the text with `#{...}`: if `name` holds `"Ada"`, then `"Hi #{name}!"` becomes `"Hi Ada!"`. This is called **string interpolation**. Double quotes also understand backslash codes such as `\n` for a new line. Single quotes, as in `'Hi #{name}'`, keep the text exactly as typed.

For several lines of text, use a **heredoc**: start with `<<~TEXT`, write the lines, and end with `TEXT` on a line of its own. The `~` removes the indentation that lines the text up with your code.

Strings come with many methods. A few you will use constantly:

- `upcase`, `capitalize`, `length` and `strip` (trims spaces at both ends).
- `include?("x")` and `start_with?("http")` answer questions.
- `split(",")` cuts the text into a list of pieces.
- `sub` and `gsub` replace the first or every occurrence: `"a-b-c".gsub("-", "+")` gives `"a+b+c"`.
- `"ab" * 3` gives `"ababab"`, and `"hello"[0]` gives `"h"`, because positions are counted from 0.
- `format("%.2f", 3.14159)` shows a number with two decimals: `"3.14"`.

Ruby strings are **mutable**: they can be changed in place. Most methods leave the original alone and hand you a new string, but `<<` (append) and the `!` methods change the string itself. After `s = "hi"`, calling `s.upcase` gives `"HI"` while `s` stays `"hi"`; calling `s.upcase!` makes `s` itself `"HI"`.

A variable does not hold its own copy of a string; it points at it. After `b = a`, both names point at the same string, so `a << "!"` changes what `b` shows too. Use `a.dup` when you want a separate copy.

To prevent surprises, many Ruby files start with the special comment `# frozen_string_literal: true`. It makes every quoted string in that file frozen, or **immutable**: it can never be changed, and trying raises a `FrozenError`. When you need a changeable string, write `+""` or `"text".dup`. Ruby is moving towards frozen strings by default, and 3.4 can warn when code changes a quoted string.

A **symbol** looks like a name with a colon in front: `:status`, `:admin`. It is a fixed label, not text to work with: the same symbol is always the very same object, and it never changes. Use symbols for names of things (you will see them as labels in collections next) and strings for text people read or type. `:ok.to_s` and `"ok".to_sym` convert between the two.
concepts.code:
# frozen_string_literal: true
name = "Ruby"
puts "Hi #{name}, #{name.length} letters"  # Hi Ruby, 4 letters
puts 'No #{interp} here'                   # No #{interp} here

text = <<~MSG
  Dear #{name},
    indented line
MSG
puts text                                  # the shared indentation is removed

p "a,b,,c".split(",")                      # ["a", "b", "", "c"]
puts "hello world".gsub("o", "0")          # hell0 w0rld
puts format("%.2f|%5s|", 3.14159, "x")     # 3.14|    x|

buf = +""            # a changeable string, even in a frozen file
buf << "a" << "b"
puts buf             # ab
puts "lit".frozen?   # true (because of the comment on line 1)
puts :ok.equal?(:ok) # true: a symbol is always the same object
takeaways: Use "#{}" to put values into text and <<~ for multi-line text
<< and ! methods change a string in place; most others return a new one
Symbols are fixed names; strings are text data
pitfalls: Changing a string through one variable and being surprised that another variable pointing at the same string changed too.

quiz.q: With # frozen_string_literal: true at the top, what happens on s = "abc"; s << "d"?
options: A new string is quietly created
quiz.explain: Quoted strings in that file are frozen, so changing one raises FrozenError; use +"abc" or dup for a changeable copy.

concepts.name: Arrays, hashes and ranges
concepts.summary: Keep many values together: ordered lists (arrays), named lookups (hashes) and ranges of values like 1..5.
concepts.why: Nearly all the data a Ruby program handles, from a list of names to a user's settings, lives in arrays and hashes.
concepts.body:
Programs often work with many values at once. An **array** is an ordered list: `nums = [3, 1, 2]`. Each item has a position number, its **index**, and counting starts at 0 (**zero-based indexing**): `nums[0]` is `3`. Negative numbers count from the end, so `nums[-1]` is `2`.

Arrays grow and shrink. `nums << 5` or `push` adds to the end, `pop` removes the last item, and `unshift` and `shift` do the same at the front. `nums[1..]` gives everything from index 1 on. Reading a missing position gives `nil`; `nums.fetch(10)` stops with an error instead, better when a missing item means something went wrong. `%w[a b c]` is a shortcut for `["a", "b", "c"]`.

A **hash** stores values under names instead of positions, like a phone book: `user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 }`. Each entry is a key (`:name`) and its value (`"Ada"`), and `user[:name]` looks it up. Writing `name:` makes the key a symbol; keys of other kinds use an arrow: `{ "id" => 1 }`. Ruby keeps entries in the order you added them.

Watch out: `:name` and `"name"` are different keys, because a symbol is not a string. So `user["name"]` gives `nil`. This is a classic source of surprise `nil`s when data arrives from outside the program.

Handling missing keys:

- `h[:missing]` gives `nil`, `h.fetch(:k)` stops with a `KeyError`, and `h.fetch(:k, 0)` gives 0 instead.
- `Hash.new(0)` makes every missing key read as 0, its **default value**. That is perfect for counting things.
- For a list per key, use `Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] }`: the code in braces runs for each new key and gives it its own empty array.
- Everyday methods: `key?`, `keys`, `values`, `delete`, `merge` (combine two hashes) and `dig(:a, :b)` (reach into a hash inside a hash).

A range like `1..5` means 1 to 5, including 5; `1...5` stops just before 5, and `1..` has no end at all. `(1..5).to_a` turns a range into an array, and `(1..5).include?(3)` checks whether a value is inside.

Two shortcuts. `first, *rest = [3, 1, 2]` puts `3` in `first` and the remaining items, as an array, in `rest`. And when a variable has the same name as a key, `{ name:, age: }` is short for `{ name: name, age: age }`.
concepts.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums << 5
p nums[-1], nums[1..2], nums[10]   # 5, [1, 2], nil
first, *rest = nums
p first, rest                      # 3, [1, 2, 5]

user = { name: "Ada", "role" => "admin" }
p user[:name], user["name"]        # "Ada", nil: a symbol is not a string
p user.fetch(:age, 0)              # 0

counts = Hash.new(0)
%w[a b a c a].each { |w| counts[w] += 1 }   # count each letter
p counts                           # {"a" => 3, "b" => 1, "c" => 1}

groups = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] }
groups[:even] << 2
p groups                           # {even: [2]}

name, age = "Bo", 7
p({ name:, age: })                 # {name: "Bo", age: 7}
p (1...4).to_a, (1..).first(2)     # [1, 2, 3], [1, 2]
takeaways: Arrays are ordered lists reached by index, counting from 0
Hashes look values up by key; symbol keys and string keys are different
Use fetch when a missing key is a bug, and Hash.new(0) for counters
pitfalls: Using Hash.new([]) to group things: every key shares one and the same array. Use the version with braces, Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] }.

quiz.q: What happens with h = Hash.new([]); h[:a] << 1; h[:b] << 2?
options: h is still empty, and the one shared default array is [1, 2]
quiz.explain: << changes the single default array without ever storing a key; use Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] } instead.

quiz.q: With nums = [4, 5, 6], what is nums[1]?
quiz.explain: Indexes count from 0, so index 1 is the second item.

concepts.name: Defining methods
concepts.summary: Write your own methods with required, optional and keyword arguments, and let the last line be the result.
concepts.why: Methods let you name a piece of work and reuse it, and keyword arguments keep the places that call them easy to read.
concepts.body:
When you need the same steps in several places, wrap them in a method of your own and give it a name. You have been calling built-in methods like `upcase`; now you define one:

```ruby
def greet(name)
  "Hello, #{name}!"
end
greet("Ada")   # gives "Hello, Ada!"
```

`def` starts the definition and `end` closes it. Other languages call a named, reusable piece of code like this a **function**.

`name` is a **parameter**: a named slot for an input. The actual value you pass in, `"Ada"`, is an **argument**. A method can take several, separated by commas.

The result a method hands back is its **return value**. In Ruby that is simply the value of the last line it runs, so you rarely write `return`; use it only to leave early, as in `return 0 if list.empty?`. A very short method can fit on one line: `def square(x) = x * x`.

Ruby offers several kinds of parameter, written in this order:

- Required: `def greet(name)`.
- With a default value, so it can be left out: `def greet(name, greeting = "Hello")`.
- `*args` gathers any extra arguments into an array. The star is called the **splat operator**.
- Keyword arguments: `def connect(host:, port: 5432)`.
- `**opts` gathers extra keyword arguments into a hash.
- `&block` accepts a chunk of code, which the next lesson explains.

**Keyword arguments** are passed by name: `connect(host: "db", port: 6543)`. The call explains itself, and the order doesn't matter. `host:` with nothing after it is required; `port: 5432` has a default. Leaving out a required one, or passing one the method doesn't know, stops with an `ArgumentError`.

Ordinary arguments, matched by their place in the list, are called **positional arguments**. If you already have a hash of settings, spread it into keyword arguments with `**`: `connect(**settings)`. Since Ruby 3.0 you must write the `**`; a hash passed without it counts as one positional argument.

Method names may end in `?` (answers yes or no), `!` (changes things in place, or is risky) or `=` (sets a value). A method can return several values in an array, and the caller can split them into separate variables: `low, high = bounds(list)`.
concepts.code:
def greet(name, greeting = "Hello", punct: "!")
  "#{greeting}, #{name}#{punct}"
end

def connect(host:, port: 5432, **opts)
  "#{host}:#{port} #{opts}"
end

def bounds(list) = [list.min, list.max]

puts greet("Ada")                       # Hello, Ada!
puts greet("Bo", "Hi", punct: "?")      # Hi, Bo?
puts connect(host: "db", ssl: true)     # db:5432 {ssl: true}

settings = { host: "cache", port: 6379 }
puts connect(**settings)                # cache:6379 {}

low, high = bounds([4, 9, 1])
puts "#{low}..#{high}"                  # 1..9

begin                                   # begin/rescue catches an error
  connect(port: 1)                      # (explained in a later lesson)
rescue ArgumentError => e
  puts e.message                        # missing keyword: :host
end
takeaways: The value of the last line is the method's return value
Keyword arguments (greeting: "Hi") make calls explain themselves
Spread a hash into keyword arguments with **
pitfalls: Passing a hash where keyword arguments are expected without writing **, which raises ArgumentError in Ruby 3.

quiz.q: Given def f(a, b: 2) whose only line is a + b, what does f(1, b: 5) return?
quiz.explain: b: 5 replaces the default for b, so the last line gives 1 + 5 = 6.

quiz.q: In def greet(name) ... end called as greet("Ada"), which is the argument?
quiz.explain: name is the parameter (the slot); "Ada" is the argument (the value put in it).

concepts.name: Blocks and iterators
concepts.summary: Hand chunks of code to methods like each, map and select, and write your own methods that run them with yield.
concepts.why: Blocks are Ruby's best-known feature: almost every loop, and every "run this code for me" in Ruby, is a block.
concepts.body:
A **block** is a chunk of code you hand to a method, so the method can run it for you: once, many times, or not at all. Write it in curly braces for one line, or between `do` and `end` for several:

```ruby
[1, 2, 3].each { |n| puts n }
[1, 2, 3].each do |n|
  puts n * 10
end
```

The method decides when to run the block and what to pass in. The names between bars, `|n|`, are the block's parameters: here `each` runs the block once per item, putting the item in `n`.

Methods like `each` that walk through a collection, running a block for every item, are called **iterators**. The core ones:

- `each` runs the block for every item and gives back the original collection.
- `map` gives back a new array of the block's results.
- `select` (or `filter`) keeps the items where the block answers yes; `reject` leaves them out.
- `find` returns the first item that matches; `any?`, `all?` and `count` answer questions.
- `each_with_index`, `each_slice(2)`, `times` and `upto` are other common ones.

Your own methods can take a block too. Inside the method, `yield` runs the caller's block, passing in any values you give it, and `block_given?` checks whether a block was passed at all.

A common Ruby habit is a method that does some setup, yields, then cleans up afterwards: opening a file before your code and closing it after, for example. Adding `ensure` (as in the example) makes the clean-up run even if the block fails.

Two shorthands: `map(&:upcase)` is short for `map { |s| s.upcase }`, and since Ruby 3.4, `it` stands for the single parameter: `nums.map { it * 2 }`.

A block can use the variables around it, and even change them: with `total = 0`, the code `nums.each { |n| total += n }` adds every number into `total`. A piece of code that remembers the variables from where it was written is called a **closure**.

Inside a block, `next` ends this run of the block early (optionally with a value), and `break` stops the whole method call.
concepts.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
p nums.map { |n| n * n }          # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
p nums.select(&:even?)            # [2, 4]
p nums.find { it > 3 }            # 4 (`it` needs Ruby 3.4)
p %w[a b].map(&:upcase)           # ["A", "B"]

def twice
  return :no_block unless block_given?
  yield 1
  yield 2
end
twice { |x| puts "got #{x}" }     # got 1 / got 2
p twice                           # :no_block

def timed(label)
  start = Time.now
  yield
ensure                            # runs even if the block fails
  puts "#{label} took #{(Time.now - start).round(3)}s"
end
timed("sum") { (1..1_000_000).sum }   # sum took 0.0s (roughly)

total = 0
nums.each { |n| total += n }      # the block changes total
p total                           # 15
takeaways: A block is code handed to a method; yield runs it
map transforms, select filters, each just walks through
&:method and it are shorthands for simple blocks
pitfalls: Using each when you want the changed values: each gives back the original array, not the block's results. Use map.

quiz.q: What does [1, 2, 3].each { |n| n * 10 } return?
quiz.explain: each gives back the collection it walked through; use map to collect the block's results.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.summary: Design your own kinds of objects with classes: set them up in initialize, keep data in @variables, expose it with attr_reader.
concepts.why: Ruby is built around objects (a style called object-oriented programming), and every larger Ruby program is made of classes.
concepts.body:
So far you have used objects that Ruby provides: strings, numbers, arrays. A **class** is a blueprint for making your own kind of object. An `Account` class describes what every account holds (whose it is, how much is in it) and what it can do (take a deposit). Ruby's own `String` is a class too.

Each object made from a class is an **instance** of it: `"hi"` is an instance of `String`. Create one of your own with `Account.new("Ada")`. That calls the class's `initialize` method, where you set up the new object. Other languages call such a set-up method a **constructor**.

Each object keeps its own data in **instance variables**, whose names start with `@`: `@owner`, `@balance`. Every method of that object can see them, but code outside the object cannot. An instance variable you never set reads as `nil`.

To let outside code read or change that data, add one-line shortcuts at the top of the class:

- `attr_reader :name` creates a method `name` that returns `@name`.
- `attr_writer :name` creates `name=`, which sets it.
- `attr_accessor :name` creates both.

Inside a method, **`self`** means "this object". To call a setter there, write `self.balance = 10`. Without `self.`, Ruby thinks you are making a new variable called `balance` that only exists inside that method: a classic bug.

Methods are public (callable from anywhere) by default. Methods listed after the word `private` can only be called from inside the object itself, which keeps helper code hidden.

A method defined as `def self.create` belongs to the class itself rather than to its instances, so you call it as `Account.create`. Constants such as `LIMIT = 100` can live inside a class too.

A class can build on another: `class Admin < User` gives Admin everything User has, and Admin can then add or change things. This is **inheritance**, and User is Admin's parent class. Inside a method, `super` calls the parent class's version of that same method.

Some method names are special. Define `to_s`, and `puts` and `"#{obj}"` will use it; define `==` to decide when two objects count as equal.

For simple objects that only hold values, `Point = Data.define(:x, :y)` creates a whole class in one line. Its instances can't be changed after they are made, and two points with the same x and y count as equal.
concepts.code:
class Account
  attr_reader :owner, :balance

  def initialize(owner, balance = 0)
    @owner = owner
    @balance = balance
  end

  def deposit(amount)
    raise ArgumentError, "amount must be positive" unless amount.positive?
    @balance += amount
    self                     # return the account so calls can be chained
  end

  def to_s = "#{owner}: #{balance}"
end

acct = Account.new("Ada").deposit(50).deposit(25)
puts acct                    # Ada: 75
p acct.respond_to?(:balance=)   # false: balance can be read, not set

Point = Data.define(:x, :y)
a = Point.new(x: 1, y: 2)
p a                          # #<data Point x=1, y=2>
p a == Point.new(1, 2)       # true: same values, so equal
p a.with(y: 5)               # #<data Point x=1, y=5> (a new point)
takeaways: Name.new creates an instance and runs initialize
@variables hold each object's own data; attr_reader and friends expose it
Inside a method, write self.attr = value to call a setter
pitfalls: Writing balance = 10 inside a method when you meant the setter: it creates a new local name. Write self.balance = 10.

quiz.q: Inside a method, what does name = "x" do when the class has attr_accessor :name?
options: Creates a new variable called name, inside this method only
quiz.explain: A bare assignment always makes a new variable; you need self.name = to call the setter.

quiz.q: What does Account.new("Ada") do first?
options: Runs the class's initialize method with "Ada"
quiz.explain: new creates the instance and passes its arguments to initialize to set it up.

concepts.name: Enumerable in depth
concepts.summary: Use Enumerable's power tools: `reduce`, `group_by`, `partition`, `tally`, `each_with_object`, `sort_by` and friends.
concepts.why: Idiomatic Ruby replaces most hand-written loops with one well-chosen Enumerable method call.
concepts.body:
**Enumerable** is a module: a named bundle of methods that a class can take in (a later lesson shows how). Its 50+ methods work for any class that defines `each`, including Array, Hash, Range, Set and your own collections. Knowing the catalogue is what makes Ruby code short.

- Summarising many values into one (**aggregation**): `sum`, `count`, `min_by`, `max_by`, `minmax`, and `reduce(:+)` or `inject(0) { |acc, x| acc + x }` for anything custom; `acc` (the accumulator) carries the running result from one step to the next.
- Grouping: `group_by { |w| w.length }` returns a hash of arrays; `partition` splits into two arrays (matches, non-matches); `tally` counts occurrences; `chunk_while` and `slice_when` split runs.
- Building: `each_with_object({}) { |x, h| ... }` passes the same accumulator to every call, and `to_h { |x| [key, value] }` builds a hash directly.
- Transforming: `flat_map`, `filter_map` (map, then leave out nils and falses, in one pass), `zip`, `each_slice(n)`, `each_cons(n)`, `uniq`.
- Ordering: `sort_by { |u| [u.last, u.first] }` sorts by several keys; `sort` uses `<=>`; `max(3)` returns the three largest.

Hashes enumerate `[key, value]` pairs, so blocks can take `|k, v|`. They also have hash-returning versions: `transform_values`, `transform_keys`, `filter_map`, `select`, `sum`, `to_h`.

Call one of these methods without a block and most return an **Enumerator**: an object that remembers the walk through the items, so you can chain another method onto it: `each_with_index.map { |x, i| ... }` or `map.with_index(1)`.
takeaways: Any class with each can include Enumerable and get 50+ methods
`group_by`, `partition`, `tally` and `each_with_object` replace hand-written loops
Block-less calls return Enumerators, enabling map.with_index and chaining
pitfalls: Using inject with a mutable accumulator but forgetting to return it from the block; use each_with_object instead.

quiz.q: What does [1, 2, 3, 4].partition(&:even?) return?
quiz.explain: partition returns two arrays: elements where the block is truthy, then the rest.

quiz.q: Why does inject({}) { |h, x| h[x] = 1 } fail on the second element?
options: The block returns 1, which becomes the next accumulator
quiz.explain: inject passes the block's return value as the next accumulator; each_with_object avoids this.

concepts.name: Modules and mixins
concepts.summary: Use modules to group names and to share methods between classes (include, extend, prepend), with Comparable and Enumerable as examples.
concepts.why: Modules are how Ruby shares behaviour across classes that aren't related by inheritance; Enumerable and Comparable are the most-used examples.
concepts.body:
A **module** is a named bundle of methods and constants. Unlike a class, you can't create objects from it: there is no `Mod.new`. It has two jobs.

As a **namespace**, it keeps names apart, like folders that each hold a file called notes.txt: `module Billing; class Invoice; end; end` is referred to as `Billing::Invoice`, so it can't clash with another `Invoice`. A **library** (ready-made code you add to your program; packaged Ruby libraries are called gems) puts everything under one top-level module for this reason.

As a **mixin**, it adds a set of methods to any class that mixes it in:

- `include Mod` adds the module's methods to every instance. To find a method, Ruby searches an ordered list of classes and modules called the **ancestor chain** (`Klass.ancestors` prints it), and `include` places the module right after the class.
- `extend Mod` adds them to one single object, usually the class itself, so they become class methods (`Klass.helper`).
- `prepend Mod` places the module *before* the class in the chain, so its methods run first and can call `super` to reach the class's own method. This is the clean way to wrap extra behaviour around existing methods.

Each mixin expects something from the class. **Comparable** needs `<=>` (which returns -1, 0 or 1 for smaller, equal or bigger) and gives you `<`, `<=`, `==`, `>`, `between?` and `clamp`. **Enumerable** needs `each` and gives you `map`, `select`, `sort`, `sum` and the rest.

`Klass.ancestors` shows the lookup order, and `obj.is_a?(Mod)` is true for included modules. A module can define `self.included(base)`, a method Ruby calls automatically when the module is included; libraries use it to add class methods at the same time. **Ruby on Rails**, the best-known Ruby framework for building websites, wraps this approach in `ActiveSupport::Concern`.

`module_function` makes utility modules whose methods are called as `Mod.method`, like `Math.sqrt`.
concepts.code:
class Version
  include Comparable
  attr_reader :parts
  def initialize(s) = @parts = s.split(".").map(&:to_i)
  def <=>(other) = parts <=> other.parts
  def to_s = parts.join(".")
end

p Version.new("1.10.0") > Version.new("1.9.3")    # true
p [Version.new("2.0"), Version.new("1.2")].max.to_s  # "2.0"

class Playlist
  include Enumerable
  def initialize(*songs) = @songs = songs
  def each(&) = @songs.each(&)
end
p Playlist.new("b", "a", "c").sort               # ["a", "b", "c"]
module Loud
  def to_s = super.upcase + "!"
end
class Version
  prepend Loud
end
puts Version.new("3.4")                          # 3.4!
p Version.ancestors.first(3)                     # [Loud, Version, Comparable]
takeaways: Modules are namespaces and mixins; you can't create objects from them
include adds instance methods, extend adds methods to one object (often the class), prepend wraps
Comparable needs <=>; Enumerable needs each
pitfalls: Including a module expecting its methods as class methods; that's extend (or the self.included method).

quiz.q: Which keyword lets a module's method run before the class's own method and call it via super?
quiz.explain: prepend places the module before the class in the ancestor chain.

quiz.q: What must a class define to get Enumerable's methods?
quiz.explain: Every Enumerable method is built on each.

concepts.name: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Raise and rescue errors (exceptions), clean up with ensure, try again with retry, and design your own family of error classes.
concepts.why: Handling errors well (exception handling) is what separates scripts that silently corrupt data from programs you can trust.
concepts.body:
When something goes wrong while a program runs, such as a missing file or text that isn't a number, Ruby creates an **exception**: an error object that stops the normal flow and travels back through the methods that were called until some code handles it. If nothing does, the program stops with an error message.

Signal one yourself with `raise ArgumentError, "bad id"` (or `raise CustomError.new(...)`). Handle it with `begin`/`rescue`/`else`/`ensure`/`end`:

- `rescue SomeError => e` handles that error class and its **subclasses** (classes that inherit from it), with the error object in `e`; list several classes or several `rescue` lines, most specific first.
- `else` runs when no exception occurred.
- `ensure` always runs, which makes it the place for cleanup.
- `retry` inside `rescue` runs the `begin` part again, useful when a failure may be temporary; always cap the number of attempts.

Method bodies and `do ... end` blocks act as an implicit `begin`, so you can put `rescue` and `ensure` directly in a `def`.

The family tree of error classes matters. A bare `rescue` catches **StandardError**, the parent of ordinary program errors, and its subclasses: `ArgumentError`, `TypeError`, `NameError`, `NoMethodError`, `ZeroDivisionError`, `KeyError`, `IOError` and nearly everything an application raises. It deliberately does not catch `Exception` subclasses like `Interrupt` (Ctrl-C), `SystemExit` or `NoMemoryError`. Never write `rescue Exception` except at the very top level of a program, to log a crash.

Define your own errors by inheriting from `StandardError`, usually under one parent class per library, a package of reusable code (`MyGem::Error`), so callers can rescue all of them at once. Wrapping a low-level error inside `rescue` automatically sets the new error's `cause`, preserving the original.

The one-line modifier `value = Integer(s) rescue 0` exists but hides all StandardErrors; prefer explicit handling.
concepts.code:
class ShopError < StandardError; end
class OutOfStock < ShopError
  def initialize(item) = super("#{item} is out of stock")
end

def buy(item, stock)
  raise OutOfStock, item if stock.fetch(item).zero?
  stock[item] -= 1
end

stock = { tea: 1, cake: 0 }
%i[tea cake pie].each do |item|
  buy(item, stock)
  puts "bought #{item}"           # bought tea
rescue ShopError => e
  puts "shop: #{e.message}"       # shop: cake is out of stock
rescue KeyError
  puts "unknown item #{item}"     # unknown item pie
end
def with_log(name)
  yield
ensure
  puts "closed #{name}"           # runs even when the block raises
end
with_log("db") { Integer("42") }   # closed db
takeaways: rescue without a class catches StandardError, not Exception
ensure always runs; use it for cleanup
Give each library one Error base class subclassing StandardError
pitfalls: Writing rescue Exception, which also traps Ctrl-C and exit.

quiz.q: Which exception does a bare rescue NOT catch?
quiz.explain: Interrupt inherits from Exception (via SignalException), not StandardError.

concepts.name: Procs, lambdas and closures
concepts.summary: Store code in objects with procs and lambdas, know how the two differ, and pass methods around like values.
concepts.why: Code stored in a variable can be handed around and run later: that is how callbacks (code you give to something else to run when an event happens) and most Ruby configuration work.
concepts.body:
A block is not an object, but you can capture one. Declaring `&block` as the last parameter turns the caller's block into a **proc object** (a proc for short) holding that code, which you can store and call later with `block.call(x)` or `block.(x)`. The reverse, `&proc` at a call site, passes a Proc as a block.

Create callables directly:

- `square = ->(x) { x * x }` is a **lambda**, a small nameless function (the `lambda { |x| }` form also works).
- `Proc.new { |x| ... }` or `proc { |x| ... }` creates a plain proc.

They differ in two ways:

- **Arity**, the number of arguments expected: lambdas check it like methods do; procs are lenient, filling missing arguments with nil and ignoring extras.
- **return**: in a lambda, `return` exits the lambda. In a proc, `return` returns from the *method where the proc was defined*, and raises `LocalJumpError` if that method has already finished.

So lambdas behave like nameless methods and are the usual choice for code you store to run later.

All of them are **closures**: they keep access to the variables that existed where they were created, even after the method that created them has finished. That's how the counter in the example works.

`obj.method(:name)` returns a `Method` object, and `&` converts it too: `%w[1 2].map(&method(:Integer))`. Callables chain with `>>` and `<<`: `(f >> g).call(x)` means `g.call(f.call(x))`. `curry` makes a version that accepts its arguments a few at a time.
concepts.code:
square = ->(x) { x * x }
inc = proc { |x| (x || 0) + 1 }

p square.(4)                  # 16
p inc.call                    # 1 (procs are lenient about args)
begin
  square.call
rescue ArgumentError => e
  puts e.message              # wrong number of arguments (given 0, expected 1)
end

def make_counter
  count = 0
  -> { count += 1 }           # closes over count
end
c = make_counter
c.call; c.call
p c.call                      # 3

def run(&block) = block.call(10)
p run { it / 2 }              # 5
p %w[1 2 3].map(&method(:Integer))   # [1, 2, 3]
pipeline = square >> inc >> :to_s.to_proc
p pipeline.call(3)            # "10"
p [square.lambda?, inc.lambda?]      # [true, false]
takeaways: &block captures a block as a Proc; &callable passes one as a block
Lambdas check arity and return locally; procs do neither
All are closures over the variables where they were created
pitfalls: Using return inside a proc that outlives its method, causing LocalJumpError.

quiz.q: A method defines pr = proc { return 1 }, calls pr.call, then has puts "after". What happens?
options: The proc returns 1 and the method continues
The method returns 1 immediately; after is not printed
quiz.explain: return in a proc returns from the enclosing method, so the rest of the method is skipped.

concepts.name: Pattern matching
concepts.summary: Unpack arrays and hashes with case/in, guards, pins and find patterns, and use => and in as one-liners.
concepts.why: Checking the shape of nested data and pulling pieces out of it, as you do with data received from web services, becomes short and safe.
concepts.body:
`case`/`in` (stable since Ruby 3.0) does **pattern matching**: it checks a value against patterns that describe its shape and, in the same step, stores the parts it needs in variables:

```ruby
case response
in { status: 200, body: { user: { name: String => name } } }
  greet(name)
in { status: 404 | 410 }
  not_found
in { status: Integer => code } if code >= 500
  retry_later(code)
end
```

The pieces:

- **Value patterns** compare with `===`, so kinds of value (`Integer`), ranges (`1..5`) and text patterns (`/@/`, a **regular expression**: a mini-language for text patterns, here meaning "contains @") all work.
- **Array patterns** `[x, y]` require exact length; `[first, *rest]` captures the tail; the find pattern `[*, { id: 3 } => hit, *]` searches anywhere.
- **Hash patterns** `{ name: }` match a subset of keys and bind `name`. Use `**rest` to capture the others or `**nil` to forbid extras. They match symbol keys only.
- `|` for alternatives, `=> var` to bind a sub-pattern, `if`/`unless` guards.
- `^var` **pins** an existing variable's value instead of rebinding it: `in { id: ^expected_id }`.

If no `in` line matches and there's no `else`, Ruby raises `NoMatchingPatternError`, which surfaces unexpected data early.

One-liners: `config => { db: { host: } }` **destructures** (unpacks the parts into variables) or raises, and `value in { type: :admin }` returns true or false. Classes opt in by defining `deconstruct` and `deconstruct_keys`; `Data` and `Struct` already do.
concepts.code:
def describe(event)
  case event
  in { type: "click", pos: [x, y] } if x.negative? || y.negative?
    "click outside"
  in { type: "click", pos: [x, y] }
    "click at #{x},#{y}"
  in { type: "key", key: "a".."z" => k }
    "letter #{k}"
  in { type: String => t, **rest }
    "other #{t} with #{rest.keys}"
  end
end

puts describe({ type: "click", pos: [3, 4] })   # click at 3,4
puts describe({ type: "click", pos: [-1, 0] })  # click outside
puts describe({ type: "key", key: "q" })        # letter q
puts describe({ type: "scroll", dy: 5 })        # other scroll with [:dy]

config = { db: { host: "localhost", port: 5432 } }
config => { db: { host:, port: } }
puts "#{host}:#{port}"                          # localhost:5432

expected = 2
found = ([{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }] in [*, { id: ^expected }, *])
p found                                         # true
takeaways: case/in checks structure and binds variables in one step
Hash patterns match a subset of symbol keys; array patterns match exact length
Use ^ to pin an existing value; a value that matches nothing raises NoMatchingPatternError
pitfalls: Expecting in { x: } to match hashes with string keys, such as data read from JSON text; read it with JSON.parse(text, symbolize_names: true) to get symbol keys.

quiz.q: Does { name: "Ann", age: 30 } match the pattern in { name: String }?
options: No, hash patterns need every key listed
Yes, hash patterns match a subset of keys
quiz.explain: Hash patterns ignore extra keys unless you add **nil.

concepts.name: Gems and Bundler
concepts.summary: Install libraries as gems, list the ones a project needs in a Gemfile, record exact versions with Bundler and run with bundle exec.
concepts.why: Every real Ruby project, Rails apps included, manages the gems it needs with Bundler.
concepts.body:
A **gem** is a packaged Ruby library, published on **rubygems.org**, the public gem site. `gem install rubocop` installs one for the whole computer, and `require "json"` loads a library into your program. Ruby's **standard library**, the code that comes with Ruby itself, includes many gems already (`json` and `csv` for reading data files, `set`, `net-http` for talking to websites, `minitest` for tests).

For projects, use **Bundler**. A **Gemfile** lists the gems the project needs, its **dependencies**:

```ruby
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "faraday", "~> 2.12"
group :development, :test do
  gem "rspec", "~> 3.13"
end
```

`bundle install` picks versions that work together and writes **Gemfile.lock** with the exact version of every gem, including the gems your gems need. Keep Gemfile.lock with an application's code so every computer that runs it gets identical versions. `bundle add faraday` edits the Gemfile and installs in one step; `bundle update faraday` deliberately upgrades one gem; `bundle outdated` lists available upgrades.

The pessimistic operator `~> 2.12` means `>= 2.12` and `< 3.0`; `~> 2.12.1` means `< 2.13`.

Run commands with **`bundle exec`** (`bundle exec rspec`) so they use the locked versions, not whatever is installed globally. In code, `require "bundler/setup"` does the same. Rails apps include small scripts called **binstubs**, like `bin/rails`, that do it for you.

A library you publish is described by a `.gemspec`; `bundle gem name` generates a starter project for one. Version managers such as rbenv, chruby, asdf or mise switch Ruby versions per project via `.ruby-version`.
concepts.code:
# Shell session
bundle init                       # creates a Gemfile
bundle add faraday --version "~> 2.12"
bundle add rspec --group "development,test"
bundle install                    # writes Gemfile.lock

cat Gemfile.lock | grep -A1 "faraday ("   # exact resolved version

bundle exec ruby -e 'require "faraday"; puts Faraday::VERSION'
bundle outdated                   # what could be upgraded
bundle update faraday             # upgrade just this gem (within ~>)

echo "3.4.7" > .ruby-version      # picked up by rbenv / chruby / mise
bundle gem my_tool                # scaffold a publishable gem
takeaways: Gemfile declares dependencies; Gemfile.lock pins exact versions
Keep Gemfile.lock with an application's code
Use bundle exec (or binstubs) to run with the locked versions
pitfalls: Running a tool without bundle exec and getting a different global version than the project expects.

quiz.q: What range does gem "rack", "~> 3.1" allow?
quiz.explain: ~> with two segments allows the last one to grow, so >= 3.1 and < 4.0.

concepts.name: Files, IO and the standard library
concepts.summary: Read and write files safely with blocks, work with file paths, and read JSON and CSV data with tools that come with Ruby.
concepts.why: Scripting and data jobs, one of Ruby's strengths, are mostly reading, transforming and writing files.
concepts.body:
Reading and writing files is most of what scripts do. The simplest file operations are one-liners: `File.read(path)` returns the whole content, `File.write(path, text)` replaces it, and `File.readlines(path, chomp: true)` returns an array of lines. They are fine for small files.

For anything larger or longer-lived, use the **block form** of `File.open`, which closes the file even if an exception is raised:

```ruby
File.open("out.log", "a") { |f| f.puts "started" }
```

Modes: `"r"` read (default), `"w"` truncate and write, `"a"` append, `"r+"` read and write; add `"b"` for **binary** files (raw bytes such as images, not text). `File.foreach(path) { |line| ... }` reads one line at a time, so even a huge file never has to fit in **memory**, the computer's short-term working space, all at once.

Paths, a file's address such as `data/x.csv`: `File.join("data", "x.csv")`, `File.exist?`, `File.basename`, `File.extname`, `Dir.glob("logs/**/*.log")` (find files whose names fit a wildcard like `*.log`), and the `Pathname` class, which wraps a path in an object with methods. `__dir__` is the **directory** (folder) of the current file, useful for finding data next to a script.

Ruby's **standard library**, code that ships with Ruby and is loaded with `require`, has helpers you will use constantly:

- `require "json"` for **JSON**, the common text format for data like `{"name": "Ada"}`. To **parse** text is to read it and turn it into Ruby data: `JSON.parse(text, symbolize_names: true)`. `obj.to_json` or `JSON.pretty_generate(obj)` go the other way.
- `require "csv"` for **CSV**, a spreadsheet saved as text: each line holds one entry, with commas between its values: `CSV.foreach(path, headers: true) { |row| row["email"] }`. Since Ruby 3.4 csv is packaged separately, so Bundler projects must list it in their Gemfile.
- `require "fileutils"`: `mkdir_p`, `cp`, `rm_rf`.

Every program also has three standard places to read and write: `$stdin` (input, usually the keyboard), `$stdout` (normal output) and `$stderr`, called **standard error**, for error messages. `warn "msg"` writes to `$stderr`, and `ARGV` holds the **command-line arguments**: the extra words typed after the script name, as in `ruby tool.rb data.csv`.
concepts.code:
require "json"
require "tmpdir"

Dir.mktmpdir do |dir|
  path = File.join(dir, "people.jsonl")
  File.open(path, "w") do |f|
    f.puts({ name: "Ada", langs: %w[ruby c] }.to_json)
    f.puts({ name: "Bo", langs: %w[go] }.to_json)
  end

  people = File.foreach(path).map { JSON.parse(it, symbolize_names: true) }
  p people.first                         # {name: "Ada", langs: ["ruby", "c"]}
  p people.sum { it[:langs].size }       # 3

  File.write(File.join(dir, "summary.json"), JSON.pretty_generate(people))
  p Dir.glob("#{dir}/*").map { File.basename(it) }.sort
  # ["people.jsonl", "summary.json"]
  p File.extname(path)                   # ".jsonl"
end
takeaways: Use File.open with a block so files are always closed
File.foreach reads large files line by line
JSON.parse(text, symbolize_names: true) gives symbol keys
pitfalls: Calling File.open without a block and forgetting to close the file.

quiz.q: Why prefer File.open(path) { |f| ... } over f = File.open(path)?
options: The file is closed automatically, even when an exception occurs
It reads the whole file at once
quiz.explain: The block form ensures close in an ensure clause when the block finishes.

concepts.name: Testing with Minitest and RSpec
concepts.summary: Write automated tests with Minitest's assert methods and RSpec's describe/it/expect style, and swap real objects for stand-ins.
concepts.why: Ruby's dynamic nature makes tests the main safety net, and the community treats them as non-negotiable.
concepts.body:
An automated test is code that runs your code and checks the result, so a mistake shows up the moment you make it. Ruby has two dominant testing **frameworks**: libraries that find your tests, run them and report the results.

**Minitest** ships with Ruby (as a bundled gem) and is what Rails uses by default. Tests are classes inheriting from `Minitest::Test`, and every method starting with `test_` is a test:

- Each check is an **assertion**: it fails the test if its condition isn't true. `assert_equal expected, actual`, `assert`, `refute`, `assert_nil`, `assert_includes`, and `assert_in_delta` for floats.
- `assert_raises(KeyError) { ... }` returns the exception so you can check its message.
- `setup` and `teardown` run around each test.

Run a file with `ruby -Itest test/cart_test.rb`, or through Rake or Rails. Minitest also has a `describe`/`it` style and simple **mocks** and stubs: stand-in objects that replace real ones during a test (`Object#stub` from `minitest/mock`).

**RSpec** is the other big choice. Its tests read like sentences, written in a small language of its own (a **domain-specific language**, or DSL):

```ruby
RSpec.describe Cart do
  it "sums prices" do
    expect(Cart.new([2, 3]).total).to eq(5)
  end
end
```

It offers rich matchers (`eq`, `include`, `raise_error`, `change { }.by(1)`), `let` for **test fixtures** (prepared test data, built only when a test first uses it), `before` hooks, shared examples, and stand-in objects called doubles (`instance_double(Mailer, deliver: true)`), which check that the methods they fake really exist.

Whichever you pick: test behaviour through public methods, and keep each test independent. Prefer **dependency injection**, passing collaborators in as arguments so a test can hand in a stand-in, over replacing methods for the whole program. Run the tests in random order (both do by default) to expose tests that secretly depend on each other.
concepts.code:
# test_cart.rb: run with `ruby test_cart.rb`
require "minitest/autorun"

class Cart
  def initialize(prices) = @prices = prices
  def total = @prices.sum
  def item(i) = @prices.fetch(i)
end

class CartTest < Minitest::Test
  def setup
    @cart = Cart.new([2, 3.5])
  end

  def test_total
    assert_in_delta 5.5, @cart.total
  end

  def test_missing_item_raises
    err = assert_raises(IndexError) { @cart.item(9) }
    assert_match(/index 9/, err.message)
  end
end
# 2 runs, 4 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips
takeaways: Minitest is built in: subclass Minitest::Test and write test_ methods
RSpec uses describe/it/expect with rich matchers and verified doubles
Tests run in random order, so keep them independent
pitfalls: Putting the actual value first in assert_equal, which makes failure messages misleading.

quiz.q: In Minitest, what is the argument order of assert_equal?
quiz.explain: assert_equal expected, actual; swapping them produces confusing failure messages.

concepts.name: The object model
concepts.summary: Understand singleton classes, method lookup through ancestors, self, and how class methods really work.
concepts.why: Every piece of Ruby metaprogramming, and much Rails magic, follows directly from the object model.
concepts.body:
In Ruby, classes are objects too: `User` is an instance of `Class`, which inherits from `Module`, which inherits from `Object`. Everything else follows from a few rules.

**Method lookup**: when you call `obj.foo`, Ruby looks in obj's **singleton class** (explained below), then its class, then each entry of `obj.class.ancestors` in order: prepended modules, the class, included modules (most recent first), the superclass, and so on up to `Object`, `Kernel` and `BasicObject`. The first match wins; `super` continues from there. If nothing is found, Ruby calls `method_missing`, which raises `NoMethodError` by default.

**Singleton classes**: every object can have its own hidden class holding methods for that object alone, called **singleton methods**. `def obj.shout` or `obj.extend(Mod)` puts methods there. **Class methods** are simply singleton methods of the class object: `def self.create` inside `class User` defines `create` on User's singleton class. `class << self` opens that singleton class directly. Singleton classes of classes inherit from each other, which is why a **subclass** (a class that inherits from another) also gets its parent's class methods.

**self** changes with context: inside a class body it is the class, inside an instance method it is the instance. Calling a method without an explicit **receiver** (the object before the dot) sends it to `self`, and `private` methods can only be called that way.

Open classes let you reopen any class, even `String`, and add methods. This **monkey patching** changes the class for the whole program, which is powerful and dangerous. Prefer **refinements**, changes that apply only in files that switch them on with `using`, or plain functions.
concepts.code:
module Greet
  def hi = "hi from Greet"
end

class Base
  def hi = "hi from Base"
end

class Child < Base
  include Greet
  def hi = "Child -> " + super
  def self.build = new        # singleton method of the Child object
end

p Child.ancestors.take(4)     # [Child, Greet, Base, Object]
puts Child.new.hi             # Child -> hi from Greet

obj = Child.build
def obj.hi = "only me"        # singleton method on one instance
puts obj.hi                   # only me
puts Child.new.hi             # Child -> hi from Greet
p obj.singleton_methods       # [:hi]

p Child.singleton_class.superclass   # #<Class:Base>
p Child.class, Class.superclass      # Class, Module
takeaways: Lookup goes singleton class, then ancestors in order; first match wins
Class methods are singleton methods on the class object
Calls without a receiver go to self; private methods require that
pitfalls: Monkey patching built-in classes for the whole program, so two gems' changes can clash.

quiz.q: Where does Ruby store a method defined with def self.find inside class User?
quiz.explain: def self.x defines a singleton method on the User class object, i.e. in its singleton class.

concepts.name: Metaprogramming
concepts.summary: Generate methods with define_method, call them dynamically with send, and handle unknown calls with method_missing.
concepts.why: Metaprogramming is behind attr_accessor, the automatic methods Rails models (ActiveRecord) get and most Ruby mini-languages.
concepts.body:
Ruby lets code write code while the program is running, and the core tools are ordinary methods.

- `public_send(:name, *args)` calls a method chosen while the program runs. `send` does the same but also reaches private methods, so prefer `public_send`.
- `define_method(:name) { |args| ... }` creates a method from a block. Because the block is a closure, generated methods can capture loop variables, which is how shortcuts like `attr_accessor` are built.
- `instance_variable_get(:@x)` and `instance_variable_set` read and write state by name.
- `respond_to?(:name)` and `method_defined?` check for methods.

A class **macro** (a one-line shortcut that expands into more code, like `attr_accessor`) is just a class method called in the class body. When `has_flag :admin` runs, `self` is the class, so the macro can call `define_method` to add methods.

`method_missing(name, *args)` is called when lookup fails. It can implement dynamic finders or wrapper objects that pass calls on to another object, but always pair it with `respond_to_missing?`, call `super` for names you don't handle, and consider defining real methods on first use instead, which is faster and plays well with introspection.

Methods Ruby calls automatically let classes react to events: `inherited(subclass)`, `included(base)`, `method_added(name)`.

`instance_eval` and `class_eval` run a block with a different `self`; `class_eval` can also take Ruby code as a string and run it. That gives the fastest generated methods, but it is dangerous with **untrusted input** (text from outside your program), since it would run whatever the text says. Use these tools sparingly: metaprogrammed code is harder to search, debug and check with type checkers (tools that check values have the right kinds).
concepts.code:
class Model
  def self.flags(*names)
    names.each do |n|
      define_method("#{n}?") { @flags.include?(n) }
      define_method("#{n}!") { @flags << n; self }
    end
  end
  def initialize = @flags = []
end
class User < Model
  flags :admin, :verified
end
u = User.new.admin!
p [u.admin?, u.verified?]                 # [true, false]
p u.public_send(:verified?)               # false
class Settings
  def initialize(h) = @h = h
  def method_missing(name, *args)
    @h.key?(name) ? @h[name] : super
  end
  def respond_to_missing?(name, priv = false) = @h.key?(name) || super
end
s = Settings.new(theme: "dark")
p s.theme, s.respond_to?(:theme)          # "dark", true
begin; s.font; rescue NoMethodError; puts "no font"; end   # no font
takeaways: define_method plus closures generate methods from data
Prefer public_send to send so private methods stay private
Pair method_missing with respond_to_missing? and call super
pitfalls: Implementing method_missing without calling super, which silently swallows typos.

quiz.q: Why should method_missing call super for names it doesn't handle?
options: So unknown calls still raise NoMethodError instead of returning nil
quiz.explain: super reaches BasicObject#method_missing, which raises the normal NoMethodError.

concepts.name: Enumerators and lazy evaluation
concepts.summary: Build custom Enumerators, step through them by hand with next, and handle endless or huge sequences lazily.
concepts.why: Lazy chains handle huge files and endless sequences without building giant in-between arrays.
concepts.body:
An **Enumerator** is an object that represents an iteration. You get one by calling an iterator without a block (`[1, 2].each`, `5.times`, `File.foreach(path)`), or build one from scratch:

```ruby
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|
  a, b = 0, 1
  loop { y << a; a, b = b, a + b }
end
```

Enumerators include Enumerable, so `fib.take(10)` works even though the sequence is infinite: the block that produces values only runs as far as needed. They also let you step through by hand (**external iteration**): `e.next` returns the next value and raises `StopIteration` at the end, which `loop` rescues for you. `peek` looks ahead and `rewind` restarts.

Normally each Enumerable step builds a full intermediate array: `map` runs over everything, then `select` runs over the result. Calling `lazy` switches to **lazy evaluation**, doing work only when a result is actually needed: the chain becomes an `Enumerator::Lazy`, which pulls one element at a time through all the steps:

```ruby
(1..Float::INFINITY).lazy.map { it * 2 }.select { it % 3 == 0 }.first(3)
```

Nothing runs until a finishing method such as `first(n)`, `to_a`, `each` or `force` asks for values. Use lazy chains for infinite sources, huge files (`File.foreach(path).lazy`) and when you only need the first few results. For small arrays, the normal **eager** version (each step finishes completely before the next starts) is usually faster, because laziness adds a little extra work per element.

`Enumerator.produce(initial) { |prev| next_value }` (Ruby 2.7) is a concise way to generate sequences.
concepts.code:
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|
  a, b = 0, 1
  loop { y << a; a, b = b, a + b }
end
p fib.take(8)                       # [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]
p fib.lazy.select(&:even?).first(4) # [0, 2, 8, 34]

e = %w[a b].each
p e.next, e.next                    # "a", "b"
begin
  e.next
rescue StopIteration
  puts "done"                       # done
end

calls = 0
result = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .map { calls += 1; it * it }
  .reject(&:odd?)
  .first(3)
p result, calls                     # [4, 16, 36], 6

p Enumerator.produce(1) { it * 3 }.take(5)   # [1, 3, 9, 27, 81]
takeaways: Iterators called without a block return Enumerators
Enumerator.new and Enumerator.produce build custom, even infinite, sequences
lazy pulls elements through the chain one at a time when a finishing call like first(n) asks
pitfalls: Calling map on an endless range without lazy: it tries to build an endless array and never finishes.

quiz.q: What does (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy.map { it * 2 } return?
options: An Enumerator::Lazy; nothing is computed yet
quiz.explain: Lazy chains build a description of the work; only a finishing method like first(n) runs it.

concepts.name: Building DSLs with blocks
concepts.summary: Combine blocks, instance_eval and method chaining to build readable mini-languages (DSLs) like Rails routes and RSpec tests.
concepts.why: Much of the Ruby ecosystem (Rails routes, RSpec, Gemfiles, Rake) is a block-based DSL; knowing the trick demystifies them.
concepts.body:
A **domain-specific language** (DSL) is a small language made for one job. An internal DSL is plain Ruby shaped to read like such a language. Rails routes, **RSpec** tests (a popular testing library), Rake tasks, Gemfiles and Sinatra apps are all DSLs. They rely on three features you already know: optional parentheses, blocks, and changing `self`.

The key trick is `instance_eval(&block)` (or `instance_exec(args, &block)`): it runs the caller's block with `self` set to a builder object, so bare method calls inside the block go to the builder:

```ruby
Router.draw do
  get "/users", to: "users#index"
end
```

Here `get` is a method on the builder, not on the code that wrote the block.

The trade-off is that inside the block, `self` is no longer the caller's object, so the caller's instance variables and methods disappear (**local variables**, created in the surrounding code, still work, since the block is a closure). For that reason many libraries offer a second form that yields the builder explicitly, `config do |c| c.port = 80 end`, which keeps `self` unchanged. Supporting both is easy: check `block.arity`.

Design tips:

- Keep the DSL small and make each method do one obvious thing.
- Store what the block declares and act on it later; don't do heavy work during evaluation.
- Check input as soon as it arrives and raise clear errors that name the DSL method.
- Use `Module#refine` (refinements, activated with `using`) rather than monkey patching if the DSL needs extra methods on core classes such as `5.minutes`.
concepts.code:
class RouteSet
  Route = Data.define(:verb, :path, :target)

  def self.draw(&block)
    set = new
    block.arity == 1 ? block.call(set) : set.instance_eval(&block)
    set.routes
  end
  attr_reader :routes
  def initialize = @routes = []
  %w[get post].each do |verb|
    define_method(verb) { |path, to:| @routes << Route.new(verb.upcase, path, to) }
  end
  def resources(name) = [get("/#{name}", to: "#{name}#index"), post("/#{name}", to: "#{name}#create")]
end

prefix = "/api"
routes = RouteSet.draw do
  get "#{prefix}/health", to: "health#show"   # locals still visible
  resources :users
end
routes.each { |r| puts "#{r.verb} #{r.path} -> #{r.target}" }
# GET /api/health -> health#show
# GET /users -> users#index
# POST /users -> users#create
takeaways: instance_eval runs a block with self set to a builder object
Inside such blocks, locals still work but the caller's methods and ivars don't
Offer a yield-the-builder form when callers need their own self
pitfalls: Referencing @ivars of the calling object inside an instance_eval block; they belong to the builder there.

quiz.q: Inside Router.draw { get "/x" } implemented with instance_eval, which object receives get?
options: The builder object that instance_eval runs on
quiz.explain: instance_eval changes self to the builder, so receiverless calls go to it.

concepts.name: Threads, the GVL and Ractors
concepts.summary: Use threads, Mutex and Queue to wait on many things at once, understand the GVL, and know what Ractors offer for true parallelism.
concepts.why: Ruby web servers like Puma, job runners like Sidekiq and every concurrent Ruby service depend on how threads and the GVL behave.
concepts.body:
A **thread** is one line of work inside a running program. With several threads, a program makes progress on several tasks during the same stretch of time: **concurrency**, such as waiting on many web requests at once. Doing work at literally the same instant on several CPU cores is **parallelism**.

`Thread.new { ... }` starts a thread managed by the operating system; `join` waits for it and `value` returns the block's result. Threads share memory, so data that several of them change (**shared state**) needs protection. A **mutex** is a lock only one thread can hold at a time: `lock.synchronize { ... }`.

Often better is to pass work through a **queue**, a first-in, first-out line: Ruby's `Queue` is safe to use from many threads at once. `SizedQueue` has a size limit, so a fast producer waits for slow consumers (**backpressure**).

**CRuby**, the standard Ruby, has a **Global VM Lock (GVL)**: only one thread runs Ruby code at a time (per Ractor, below). Consequences:

- Threads give real speedups for **I/O-bound** work: work that mostly waits for **I/O** (input and output: files, databases, the network). A waiting thread releases the GVL, as do `sleep` and most **C extensions** (gem parts written in C), so ten threads can wait on ten web requests at once. That is why Puma and Sidekiq keep a **thread pool**, a fixed set of reusable threads.
- **CPU-bound** Ruby code, busy calculating rather than waiting, does not get faster with threads. Use several **processes** instead (separate running copies of the program, like Puma's workers or `fork`), or Ractors.
- The GVL is not a substitute for locking: `count += 1` is a read, an add and a write, and a switch to another thread can happen between them.

**Ractors** (experimental since 3.0) are independent units that truly run in parallel, each with its own GVL. They can't share changeable objects: you send messages (copied, or handed over entirely), and only deeply frozen objects cross freely. In 3.4 you exchange values with `send`/`receive` and get a result with `take`. Many gems are not Ractor-safe yet, so treat them as an option for isolated CPU work.

Other hazards: `Thread#raise` and `Timeout.timeout` interrupt code at arbitrary points, and an exception in a thread is only re-raised when you `join` it (`Thread.report_on_exception`, on by default, logs it).
takeaways: The GVL lets only one thread run Ruby code at a time; I/O releases it
Threads speed up I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound Ruby
Protect shared state with Mutex or pass work through Queue
pitfalls: Assuming the GVL makes counter += 1 thread-safe; it can still lose updates.

quiz.q: A CPU-heavy pure-Ruby computation is split across 4 threads in CRuby. What speedup do you expect?
quiz.explain: The GVL serialises Ruby execution, so CPU-bound threads take turns; use processes or Ractors for parallelism.

quiz.q: Why do threads help a script that fetches 20 URLs?
options: Blocking I/O releases the GVL, so other threads run while one waits
The GVL is disabled for network code
quiz.explain: While a thread waits on the network it releases the GVL, letting the others proceed.

concepts.name: Fibers and the fiber scheduler
concepts.summary: Use Fibers as lightweight pausable tasks (coroutines) and see how the fiber scheduler lets ordinary code wait on many things at once.
concepts.why: The fiber scheduler lets Ruby run thousands of waiting network and file operations at once with ordinary, step-by-step code.
concepts.body:
A **Fiber** is a lightweight **coroutine**: a piece of code that can pause in the middle and be resumed later. It runs when you call `resume` and pauses itself with `Fiber.yield`, handing a value back. Fibers take turns cooperatively: each decides when to pause, and nothing interrupts it.
