They cost far less memory than threads and switch without help from the operating system. External Enumerators (`e.next`) are built on fibers.

```ruby
f = Fiber.new { x = Fiber.yield(1); x * 10 }
f.resume      # => 1 (paused at yield)
f.resume(5)   # => 50 (yield returned 5; fiber finished)
```

Ruby 3.0 added the **fiber scheduler**. Some operations normally make the whole thread wait (they are **blocking**): reading from a network connection or a pipe, `sleep`, looking up a web address (DNS), `Process.wait`, `Thread#join`. When a **non-blocking** fiber runs and a scheduler has been set with `Fiber.set_scheduler`, these operations call the scheduler instead. It parks that fiber, runs others, and resumes it when its data is ready, using the operating system's tools for watching many connections at once (epoll, kqueue or io_uring).

Ruby ships only the list of hooks a scheduler must provide; the schedulers themselves come from gems, most notably `async` (used by the Falcon web server). With it you write normal step-by-step code inside `Async do ... end` tasks and get the effect of an **event loop**, one thread juggling many waiting tasks, without callbacks or the `await` markers other languages need.

Limits: it only helps operations that go through Ruby's own I/O code or C extensions written to cooperate. CPU-bound work, or a C extension that waits without handing back control, still stalls every fiber on that thread. Fibers don't run in parallel; combine them with processes to use several CPU cores.
concepts.code:
gen = Fiber.new do
  3.times { |i| Fiber.yield "step #{i}" }
  "finished"
end
4.times { puts gen.resume }      # step 0, step 1, step 2, finished
p gen.alive?                     # false

# Round-robin of cooperative tasks
tasks = %w[A B].map do |name|
  Fiber.new do
    2.times { |i| puts "#{name}#{i}"; Fiber.yield }
    :done
  end
end
until tasks.empty?
  tasks.reject! { |t| t.resume == :done }
end
# A0 B0 A1 B1 (one per line)

# With the async gem (Fiber scheduler), these 3 sleeps overlap:
#   require "async"
#   Async { 3.times.map { Async { sleep 1 } }.each(&:wait) }  # ~1s total
takeaways: Fibers are coroutines: resume runs, Fiber.yield pauses and returns a value
The fiber scheduler turns blocking I/O calls into event-loop switches
Ruby defines the interface; gems like async implement it
pitfalls: Expecting fibers to speed up CPU-bound work; they never run in parallel.

quiz.q: With a fiber scheduler set, what happens when a non-blocking fiber calls sleep(1)?
options: The fiber is moved to a new thread
The whole thread sleeps for 1 second
The scheduler parks the fiber and runs others until the timer fires
quiz.explain: Blocking operations are routed to scheduler hooks, which switch to other ready fibers.

concepts.name: Memory, GC and object shapes
concepts.summary: Learn how CRuby reserves memory for objects, how its generational garbage collector works, and how to find allocation hot spots and leaks.
concepts.why: Runaway memory growth and garbage-collection pauses are the most common performance problems in live Ruby services.
concepts.body:
**CRuby**, the standard Ruby, keeps objects in fixed-size slots on the **heap**, the large area of memory for data whose size and lifetime aren't known in advance. Reserving memory for data is called **memory allocation**. Since Ruby 3.2, variable width allocation offers slots in several sizes (40, 80, 160, 320 and 640 bytes), so small strings and arrays fit inside their slot; bigger data gets separate memory from C's `malloc`. Immediate values (small Integers, Symbols, `nil`, `true`, `false`, most Floats on 64-bit systems) are stored directly in the reference and aren't heap objects at all.

The **garbage collector** (GC) frees memory that nothing uses any more. It is **mark-and-sweep**: it marks every object your program can still reach, then sweeps away the rest. Two optimisations:

- **Generational**: most objects die young, so frequent minor GCs scan only young objects. Objects that survive a few collections join the **old generation**, scanned only in major GCs. **Write barriers**, small checks that run when an old object is changed to point at a young one, note those links so minor GCs don't miss them.
- **Incremental** marking splits major GCs into steps to shorten pauses. `GC.compact` (or `GC.auto_compact = true`) packs objects together to close the gaps between them (fragmentation).

Tools: `GC.stat` (counts of minor and major GCs, heap pages), `ObjectSpace.count_objects`, `ObjectSpace.memsize_of`, and the `memory_profiler` and `derailed_benchmarks` gems, which find the lines that allocate the most.

Allocation is the cost you control. Freeze string literals, and avoid throwaway arrays in **hot paths** (the code that runs most often): `each` instead of `map` when you ignore the result, `sum` instead of `map.sum`, and `<<` rather than `+=` for strings. **Object shapes** (3.2) keep track of which instance variables an object has, in what order, so lookups can be cached; setting them in a consistent order, ideally all in `initialize`, keeps lookups fast for the **interpreter** (the part of Ruby that runs your code step by step) and for YJIT.

In servers running many threads, the standard C memory allocator on Linux (glibc malloc) keeps separate pools per thread and can waste a lot of memory; switching to the jemalloc allocator, or setting the environment variable `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, is a common fix.
concepts.code:
# frozen_string_literal: true
def allocations
  GC.disable
  before = GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)
  yield
  GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects) - before
ensure
  GC.enable
end

nums = (1..1000).to_a
p allocations { nums.map { it * 2 }.sum }      # 3: includes a new 1000-element array
p allocations { nums.sum { it * 2 } }          # 1: no intermediate array

p allocations { s = +""; 100.times { s << "x" } }   # ~5: appends in place
p allocations { s = ""; 100.times { s += "x" } }    # ~100: new string each time

p 42.frozen?, :sym.frozen?             # true, true (immediates)
stat = GC.stat
p stat.slice(:minor_gc_count, :major_gc_count).keys   # [:minor_gc_count, :major_gc_count]
require "objspace"
p ObjectSpace.memsize_of("x" * 10_000) > 10_000       # true
takeaways: Small integers, symbols, nil and booleans are immediates, not heap objects
The generational GC makes short-lived objects cheap but not free
Measure allocations with GC.stat and memory_profiler before optimising
pitfalls: Optimising by guesswork instead of measuring allocations in the real hot path.

quiz.q: Why is nums.sum { it * 2 } cheaper than nums.map { it * 2 }.sum?
options: It avoids allocating an intermediate array
quiz.explain: map allocates a new array of results; sum with a block accumulates directly.

quiz.q: What does a minor GC scan?
options: Mainly young objects (plus old objects recorded by write barriers)
Only objects allocated by C extensions
quiz.explain: Generational GC focuses minor collections on young objects, using remembered sets for old-to-young references.

concepts.name: YJIT and performance tuning
concepts.summary: Turn on YJIT, Ruby's just-in-time compiler, time code correctly, find slow spots with stackprof or vernier, and write code YJIT speeds up.
concepts.why: YJIT makes typical Rails apps much faster for free, and profiling tells you where the remaining time goes.
concepts.body:
**YJIT** is CRuby's **JIT compiler** (just-in-time compiler). While your program runs, it translates frequently used methods into **machine code**, the raw instructions the processor executes directly, which is much faster than the interpreter. It is written in Rust by Shopify and ready for live use since Ruby 3.2. It works by lazy basic-block versioning: it compiles each small straight-line piece of code only when that code actually runs, specialised for the kinds of values seen there. Typical Rails apps respond 15 to 30 percent faster (lower **latency**).

Enable it with `ruby --yjit`, the environment variable `RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1`, or from inside the program with `RubyVM::YJIT.enable` (3.3+). Rails 7.2+ turns it on automatically when available. Check with `RubyVM::YJIT.enabled?`, and read `RubyVM::YJIT.runtime_stats` when running with `--yjit-stats`. Compiled code takes extra memory; `--yjit-mem-size` caps it.

Code that YJIT, and the interpreter, handle well is **monomorphic**: each place that calls a method sees the same classes and object shapes every time. Set all instance variables in `initialize`, avoid redefining methods while the program runs, and keep hot paths free of `method_missing` and heavy `send`.

Measure before changing anything:

- A **benchmark** is a repeatable timing test. `benchmark-ips` reports iterations per second with error bars and warms up first, which matters with a JIT.
- A **profiler** measures where a program spends its time. Sampling profilers such as `stackprof` and `vernier` (which also shows time spent waiting for the GVL and in garbage collection) check what is running many times a second during a real workload, and `rbspy` attaches to a program that is already running.
- Often the real cost is in database queries (for example the "N+1" mistake: one query per item in a list instead of one for the whole list) or in allocations, not in running Ruby code.

Keep Ruby updated: each release brings substantial YJIT and GC improvements.
concepts.code:
# Run with: ruby --yjit bench.rb   (and compare with plain `ruby bench.rb`)
require "benchmark"

def fib(n) = n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

puts "YJIT enabled? #{!!(defined?(RubyVM::YJIT) && RubyVM::YJIT.enabled?)}"
fib(20)                                 # warm up so hot code gets compiled
t = Benchmark.realtime { fib(27) }
puts "fib(27): #{t.round(3)}s"
# Typical: interpreter ~0.20s, YJIT ~0.05s (varies by machine)

# For real comparisons use benchmark-ips:
#   require "benchmark/ips"
#   Benchmark.ips do |x|
#     x.report("map.sum") { arr.map { it * 2 }.sum }
#     x.report("sum")     { arr.sum { it * 2 } }
#     x.compare!
#   end
takeaways: Enable YJIT with --yjit, RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1 or RubyVM::YJIT.enable
Monomorphic call sites and stable object shapes JIT best
Profile with stackprof or vernier and benchmark with benchmark-ips
pitfalls: Benchmarking without a warm-up phase (running the code a while first), so JIT compilation time pollutes the measurement.

quiz.q: Why should benchmarks of YJIT-enabled code include a warm-up phase?
options: Code is compiled lazily on first runs, so early iterations measure compilation
quiz.explain: YJIT compiles hot code as it runs; measuring before it stabilises mixes compile time into results.
